concept.name: Liquidity provider
concept.definition: A liquidity provider is a market participant that supplies immediacy to a market by posting resting bids and offers — quotes or limit orders that others can trade against — rather than demanding immediate execution. Market makers are the canonical designated liquidity providers, but any participant resting limit orders in the book acts as a liquidity provider.
concept.intuition: A liquidity provider is the patient party: it posts a price and waits, letting anyone who needs to trade right now come to it — and earns the spread (or a rebate) for that patience.
concept.mechanics: The provider submits non-marketable limit orders that rest in the order book, adding displayed depth. When a liquidity taker's order executes against the resting order, the provider typically earns the spread and, on maker-taker venues, a liquidity rebate; in return it bears adverse-selection and inventory risk. Market makers formalize this role with continuous two-sided quoting obligations.
concept.failure_modes: Posted liquidity is conditional: providers cancel or widen quotes in volatile or informed-flow environments, so visible book depth can vanish in stress (flash-crash dynamics). Providing liquidity to informed flow produces systematic adverse-selection losses.
concept.misconceptions: Liquidity provision is not a charitable or risk-free activity, and not all posted quotes represent firm intent — quotes can be flickering or spoofed (the latter illegally). High displayed liquidity does not guarantee executable liquidity in size.
concept.example: A trader posts a limit order to buy 1,000 shares at $49.98 when the market is $49.98 x $50.02; when a seller's market order arrives, the resting order executes, and the venue pays the passive side a maker rebate of $0.002 per share.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
